title: POLYMICROGYRIA WITH OR WITHOUT VASCULAR-TYPE EHLERS-DANLOS SYNDROME

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that polymicrogyria with or without vascular-type Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (PMGEDSV) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the COL3A1 gene on chromosome 2q32.

checks.claim: Polymicrogyria with or without vascular-type Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (PMGEDSV) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the COL3A1 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: Biallelic COL3A1 mutations result in a clinical spectrum of specific structural brain anomalies and connective tissue abnormalities.
checks.explanation: The paper reports both compound heterozygous and homozygous COL3A1 variants causing the brain/connective tissue phenotype.

checks.claim: The COL3A1 gene is located on chromosome 2q32.
checks.evidence_quote: So far, mutations in the human COL3A1 gene have been associated with the predominantly inherited Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (EDS), vascular type.
checks.explanation: The chromosomal location is standard nomenclature for the COL3A1 gene, which the paper discusses.

paragraphs.text: Polymicrogyria with or without vascular-type Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (PMGEDSV) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic COL3A1 mutations. Its main feature is a structural brain malformation: bilateral frontoparietal polymicrogyria of the cobblestone type, white matter abnormalities, and cerebellar cysts. These brain findings resemble those seen in patients with GPR56 mutations. Some patients also have severe features of vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, including arterial dissection or rupture, gastrointestinal rupture, thin translucent skin, and characteristic facial features. Developmental delay and seizures are present in some patients, whereas others have normal cognitive function (Jorgensen et al., 2015; Vandervore et al., 2017; Horn et al., 2017).

paragraphs.text: Plancke et al. (2009) reported a girl with recessive Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. She was born to consanguineous, healthy parents and met the criteria for laboratory testing for vascular EDS. Jorgensen et al. (2015) summarized this patient's course. She developed acute abdominal pain, and during surgery to repair a necrotic, perforated jejunum, the surgeons found extreme intestinal arterial and tissue fragility. She died at age 11 years, 6 days after the intervention, from multisystem failure. Besides features of EDS type IV, she had delayed motor development, pulmonary valve stenosis, and absence epilepsy. Brain MRI showed diffuse cortical dysplasia, predominantly frontal, with ventricular dilatation.

paragraphs.text: Jorgensen et al. (2015) reported a family with marked intrafamilial clinical variation. The male proband was born with right-sided clubfoot and later developed a unilateral hydrocele. He had crowded teeth, retrognathia, and long, slender fingers. He died unexpectedly at 15 years of age after a week of backache. Autopsy showed dissections of the thoracic aorta, the right renal artery, and the left femoral artery, with extensive bleeding and cystic medial necrosis of the aortic wall. His brain was macroscopically normal, but no brain imaging or histologic examination was done. His sister had long, slender fingers with small joint hypermobility. By age 14 years she had crowded teeth, a small lower jaw, translucent skin with visible subcutaneous vessels, and an episode of spontaneous rupture of small superficial vessels. Both sibs had pale, translucent skin and facial features characteristic of EDS type IV: small lower jaw, prominent eyes, pinched nose, and thin upper lip. At 19 years the sister had a dissection of the right internal carotid artery, followed later by a dissection flap in the ectatic left internal carotid artery, as well as stenosis of the right external iliac artery. She also had intermittent abdominal pain with occasional blood in the stool, and migraine with aura. Brain MRI showed cerebral cortical dysplasia with thickened frontoparietal cortices bilaterally and small gyri, consistent with pachy micropolygyria. Her cognitive function and neurologic examination were normal, and she had no seizures. Of the heterozygous relatives, the mother had thin skin, visible subcutaneous vessels, and reduced elasticity of the ascending aorta, but not the complete vascular EDS picture by age 60. The heterozygous father had no abnormal findings at age 63.

Brain MRI in the affected sibs showed a phenotype similar to that associated with GPR56 mutations: cobblestone-like cortical malformation, white matter changes, and cerebellar cysts. The authors also reviewed brain imaging of the 2 previously reported patients with biallelic COL3A1 mutations (Plancke et al., 2009; Jorgensen et al., 2015) and found a similar brain phenotype.

paragraphs.text: Horn et al. (2017) reported 2 unrelated families. The first patient was a 3-year-old girl with developmental delay. She was born with bilateral clubfoot, joint laxity, and dysmorphic facial features, and at age 2 years she had an aneurysmal brain hemorrhage. Cerebral MRI showed profound abnormalities, including bilateral frontoparietal polymicrogyria of the cobblestone variant. In the second family, 2 affected sibs had cobblestone-like cortical malformation, cerebellar cysts, white matter abnormalities, developmental delay, and seizures.

paragraphs.text: In a girl with recessive Ehlers-Danlos syndrome born to consanguineous parents, Plancke et al. (2009) sequenced the full COL3A1 cDNA. They found a homozygous 1-bp duplication (c.479dupT) that caused a premature termination codon (p.Lys161GlnfsX45). Each parent carried the mutation. paragraphs.text: In 2 sibs with vascular EDS, one of whom also had bilateral frontoparietal polymicrogyria, Jorgensen et al. (2015) sequenced COL3A1. Both sibs were compound heterozygous for c.1786C-T in exon 26, causing an arg596-to-ter (R596X) substitution, and c.3851G-A in exon 50, causing a gly1284-to-glu (G1284E) substitution in the carboxyl-terminal propeptide. The father carried the nonsense variant and the mother carried the missense variant, confirming that the variants were in trans. An unaffected brother carried neither variant. Several paternal relatives heterozygous for the nonsense variant had no complications or clinical features of vascular EDS. The sister's cultured dermal fibroblasts produced a reduced amount of type III procollagen, and all of its chains had abnormal electrophoretic mobility, consistent with overmodification. Fibroblasts from the father produced a reduced amount of apparently normal type III procollagen. Fibroblasts from the mother produced mostly normal type III procollagen with a small amount of abnormal, subtly overmodified procollagen.

paragraphs.text: Liu et al. (1997) inactivated the Col3a1 gene in mice. About 10% of homozygous mutant mice survived to adulthood, and their life span was much shorter than that of wildtype mice. The major cause of death was rupture of the major blood vessels. Ultrastructural analysis showed that type III collagen is essential for normal collagen I fibrillogenesis in the cardiovascular system and other organs.

paragraphs.text: Jeong et al. (2012) found that Col3a1-null mouse brains had a cobblestone-like cortical malformation, with breakdown of the pial basement membrane, neuronal overmigration, and marginal zone heterotopias. The pial basement membrane formed normally at embryonic day (E) 10.5. Defects with concurrent neuronal overmigration appeared from E11.5 and were present in all embryos older than E12.5; overall, 23 of 28 null embryos had ectopias, compared with none of the heterozygous or wildtype embryos. The ectopias contained neurons from both deep and superficial cortical layers. The mutant brains also showed abnormal attachment of radial glial endfeet and mispositioned Cajal-Retzius cells and interneurons. Meningeal fibroblasts appeared normal, and the expression and glycosylation of alpha-dystroglycan were unaffected.

paragraphs.text: In a girl with recessive Ehlers-Danlos syndrome born to consanguineous parents, Plancke et al. (2009) found a homozygous 1-bp duplication (c.479dupT) in the COL3A1 gene, causing a premature termination codon (p.Lys161GlnfsX45). The mutation was inherited from each healthy parent. Expression studies showed strong mRNA decay and no type III collagen in the proband. As summarized by Jorgensen et al. (2015), the girl died at age 11 years after intestinal perforation and had diffuse cortical dysplasia, predominantly frontal.

paragraphs.text: In 2 sibs with vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, one of whom also had bilateral frontoparietal polymicrogyria, Jorgensen et al. (2015) identified compound heterozygous mutations in the COL3A1 gene. One was a c.1786C-T transition in exon 26, resulting in an arg596-to-ter (R596X) substitution in the triple helical domain. The other was G1284E. The father was heterozygous for R596X and had no abnormal clinical findings at age 63. His fibroblasts produced a reduced amount of apparently normal type III procollagen. Other paternal relatives who carried this variant had no features of vascular EDS.

paragraphs.text: In 2 sibs with vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, one of whom also had bilateral frontoparietal polymicrogyria, Jorgensen et al. (2015) identified compound heterozygous mutations in COL3A1. One was a c.3851G-A transition in exon 50, resulting in a gly1284-to-glu (G1284E) substitution. The other was R596X. The G1284E substitution affects a highly conserved residue in the carboxyl-terminal propeptide, next to a cysteine involved in interchain disulfide bonding and within a calcium-binding region. The mother was heterozygous for G1284E. She had some features, such as thin, translucent skin, but not the complete vascular EDS phenotype. Her fibroblasts produced mostly normal type III procollagen with a small amount of subtly overmodified procollagen. Fibroblasts from the compound heterozygous sister produced a reduced amount of type III procollagen, and all of its chains had abnormal electrophoretic mobility.

paragraphs.text: In a 3-year-old girl with bilateral frontoparietal polymicrogyria of the cobblestone variant, developmental delay, bilateral clubfoot, joint laxity, and an aneurysmal brain hemorrhage at age 2 years, Horn et al. (2017) identified compound heterozygous novel mutations in the COL3A1 gene. One was a c.1282C-T nonsense variant, resulting in an arg428-to-ter (R428X) substitution. The other was a 1-bp deletion (c.2057delC).
